name: Hana Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to any of it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a mobile phone network, on the line where people ring to renew their contract or complain about their bill. The contact centre is in a long low building behind the bus station, and I've been there just under a year. I do my calls, I read the offers off the screen, and I try to keep people from leaving for another network. The bit I like is the regulars, the older ladies who ask for me by name.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are you getting on there?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Not as well as I'd like, honestly. My sales numbers are low because I don't push people, and my manager keeps reminding me. There's an AI thing on the screen that tells you which offer to suggest, and I don't use it, I'd rather read the customer myself. I'm engaged to Samuel, who drives a delivery van, and we're saving for a wedding next summer at our church, but there's less than a month of money in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first of five pictures of the future. This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Well, good. I never believed all the fuss about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, to be honest, to the people at work who kept going on about it. Hard work and a good manner with people still count. I wouldn't post anything, I don't really do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even if AI does nothing, my job isn't safe. My sales numbers are low, the network is always talking about cutting costs, and there's nowhere else like it in town except the supermarket. And the wedding's going to cost more than we've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and try harder to hit my sales targets, maybe by asking the top seller on my team how she does it. I'd cut back on eating out and the nail appointments, that's about forty a month. And Samuel and I would trim the wedding list, maybe from eighty guests to fifty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, the way I already am. It's money, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't use the offer tool. Could it help your numbers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My manager says so. But I've watched people use it, and I'd rather lose a sale than sound like I'm reading a menu to a pensioner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would cutting the wedding list mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would hurt a bit, because my mother wants all her cousins there. But I'd rather have a smaller wedding than start married life in debt. My grandmother always said don't spend what you haven't got.

I'd say **hard work** and good manners with people still count.
think: Her job isn't safe because her **sales numbers** are low.
The **wedding** will cost more than the couple has saved.

Trim the **wedding list** from eighty guests to fifty.
feel: **Worried**, as she already is, about **money** rather than robots.
S0.quote: I'd rather lose a sale than sound like I'm reading a menu to a pensioner.
fieldNote: Her worry rests on **low sales** and a wedding, not on AI.
She refuses the **offer tool** because it sounds scripted.
Her grandmother's rule about **not spending** guides her choices.

steps.text: Ask the team's top seller for tips on hitting targets
Drop nail appointments and eating out to save forty a month
Cut the wedding guest list from eighty to fifty

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Answering customers. That's what I do all day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say companies should remember that customers are people, and some of them want a voice they know. I'd say it at church and at work. I wouldn't make a fuss online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job goes in that one. Contract renewals are exactly the kind of thing a computer can do, and I'm one of the lowest sellers. Samuel's van job would be all we had for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my aunt if there's a place for me at her bakery on the high street, even early mornings. I'd talk to Samuel about pushing the wedding back a year, which would break my mother's heart. And I'd stay at the phone company until they told me to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick to my stomach. Like the floor's gone soft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd stay until they tell you to go. Why not leave first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a wage is a wage, and I'm not one for jumping. My father worked twenty years at the same factory. I'd hold on until the end and then go to my aunt's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think is responsible for this, if it happens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really the computers. It's the bosses who only look at the numbers, and maybe people like me for not keeping up. I don't want handouts, I just want the chance to work.

I'd say this at **church** and at work, not online.

steps.text: Ask her aunt for early shifts at the high street bakery

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? No. That can't be right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to pray about it and look after each other, honestly. I'd say families and churches will have to step up. I wouldn't know what else to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lose my job almost straight away, I think. Samuel's van is hands-on, so he'd last until the robots in 2031, but I wouldn't have anything. I don't know anything except phones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to my aunt's bakery straight away and ask for anything. Samuel and I would cancel the wedding venue and get married quietly at church with just family. We'd probably move in with his parents to save the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked. I can't even think straight about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mother about the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That God doesn't need a big party to bless a marriage. She'd cry and then she'd start cooking for the small one. That's how she is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you look for any kind of help from the government?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if there was nothing else. I'd go to family and church first. I'd feel ashamed taking benefits, even though I know that's silly.

say: I'd say we need to **pray** and look after each other.
I'd say **families and churches** must step up.
think: She'd **lose her job** almost straight away.
Her fiancé's **van job** lasts until robots around 2031, but she'd have nothing.
do: Ask her aunt's **bakery** for any work at once.
Cancel the venue and marry **quietly at church**.
Move in with Samuel's **parents** to save rent.
S2.quote: God doesn't need a big party to bless a marriage.
fieldNote: Faith and **family** are her first response, not government help.
She feels **ashamed** at the thought of benefits.
She sees the **three-year robot gap** only through her fiancé's job.

steps.text: Ask her aunt for any job at the bakery
Cancel the wedding venue and marry quietly at church
Move in with her fiancé's parents
Lean on family and church for food and support

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's still fast, but it's not tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should get ready, learn a trade, keep their families close. I'd say that at church. I wouldn't be one of those shouting at the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably lose the phone job around 2029, maybe earlier with my numbers. The bakery is hands-on, so I'd have until the robots around 2034. That's something, at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start doing Saturday mornings at my aunt's bakery this year, to learn the ovens and the till. Samuel and I would still get married, but smaller, with fifty guests. I'd keep the phone job until they let me go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but I can breathe a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you see yourself running the bakery one day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. My aunt has no children and she's getting tired, so I could take over the bakery one day. If I learned it properly, that would be family work, which I'd like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would robots in the bakery mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can't picture it. A robot kneading dough? But if it comes, I'd be thirty-five and I'd have to think again.

say: I'd tell people to **get ready**, learn a trade and keep **family** close.
I wouldn't **shout at the government** about it.
think: She'd lose the phone job around **2029**, or earlier.
The **bakery** is hands-on and lasts until about 2034.
do: Do **Saturday mornings** at her aunt's bakery this year.
Marry Samuel with a **smaller wedding** of fifty guests.
Keep the **phone job** until she's let go.
S3.quote: My aunt has no children and she's getting tired, so I could take over the bakery one day.
fieldNote: The bakery offers a **family business** path she finds meaningful.
She still waits to be **let go** rather than leaving first.

steps.text: Work Saturday mornings learning the ovens at her aunt's bakery
Hold a smaller wedding with fifty guests
Keep the phone renewals job until she's let go

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a long time. Who knows what'll happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, and people should work hard and plan, like always. I'd say young people should learn a trade. I wouldn't change much about what I say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I probably wouldn't do anything for a while. The phone job might go by 2030 anyway, because renewals are easy for a computer. But I'd tell myself there's plenty of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have the wedding as planned next summer, maybe a bit smaller. I'd keep my phone job and try to improve my numbers. In a few years I'd think about the bakery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I'd push it to the back of my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the phone job might go by 2030 anyway. Doesn't that make ten years shorter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, it does, when you say it like that. I suppose I'd be fooling myself a bit, like my mother does with her blood pressure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you act sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If people at work started getting letters. Or if my aunt said she needed help now. Then I'd move.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd lose my job and the wedding all at once. What would help is apprenticeships for grown-ups, so people like me can learn a trade with a wage. Not handouts, a proper start.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about family. Everyone talks about jobs, but for me it's about whether my fiancé and I can get married and start a home. That's what I'm really worried about losing.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about jobs, but for me it's about whether my fiancé and I can get married and start a home.
portrait: Hana is a **27-year-old** agent on a mobile network's **renewals and complaints** line, with low sales numbers.
She is engaged to a **van driver** and saving for a church wedding, with under a month of money.
She is **traditional**, puts faith and family first, and wants work rather than handouts.
She refuses the **offer tool** and tends to hold on until she's told to go.
Her aunt's **bakery** is her hands-on fallback in every faster picture.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture, because she'd lose her job and the **wedding** at once.
whatWouldHelp: **Apprenticeships for adults**, so she can learn a trade on a wage.
